title: Physicists
body:
A team of physicists has announced the discovery of a novel superconducting material that appears to violate time‑reversal symmetry—a fundamental property of most known superconductors. The breakthrough, achieved under ultra‑low temperatures approaching absolute zero, could reshape theoretical models of quantum materials and pave the way for next‑generation technologies that exploit exotic quantum states.

The researchers, working at a national laboratory in collaboration with several universities, synthesized a crystalline compound containing heavy elements and rare‑earth ions. When cooled to just a few millikelvins, the material entered a superconducting phase in which electric current flows without resistance, as expected. However, precise magnetic measurements revealed a spontaneous internal magnetic field that persisted even in the absence of an external magnet. This internal field is a hallmark of broken time‑reversal symmetry, meaning the superconducting state distinguishes between forward and backward directions in time—a phenomenon never observed in conventional superconductors.

Time‑reversal symmetry is a cornerstone of most physical laws, dictating that processes should look the same if the direction of time is reversed. In superconductivity, the electron pairs (Cooper pairs) that carry current typically form in a way that preserves this symmetry. The new material, by contrast, appears to host a “chiral” superconducting state where the pairing mechanism itself carries an intrinsic angular momentum. This gives rise to tiny circulating currents within the crystal lattice, generating the detectable magnetic signature. The finding aligns with long‑standing theoretical predictions about so‑called “p‑wave” or “d‑wave” superconductors, but experimental verification has remained elusive—until now.

The discovery was made possible by a combination of advanced crystal‑growth techniques and ultra‑sensitive magnetometry. The team employed a dilution refrigerator to reach temperatures colder than the cosmic microwave background, ensuring that thermal fluctuations could not mask the subtle magnetic effects. Simultaneously, a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) array measured the minuscule magnetic fields with a resolution of a few nanoteslas. By systematically varying the temperature and magnetic field, the researchers mapped out a phase diagram that clearly demarcated the symmetry‑broken superconducting region.

Beyond its fundamental significance, the material could have practical implications for quantum computing and spintronics. Superconductors that break time‑reversal symmetry are predicted to host Majorana quasiparticles—exotic excitations that can encode information in a way that is inherently protected from decoherence. Harnessing such particles could lead to fault‑tolerant quantum bits, dramatically improving the stability of quantum processors. Moreover, the intrinsic magnetic texture of the material may enable new types of low‑power electronic devices that manipulate electron spin without external magnetic fields, a long‑sought goal in spintronic engineering.

Nevertheless, challenges remain before the discovery can be translated into technology. The necessity of millikelvin temperatures makes large‑scale applications impractical with current cooling infrastructure. Researchers will need to explore chemical substitutions, pressure tuning, or interface engineering to raise the critical temperature while preserving the symmetry‑breaking properties. Additionally, confirming the presence of Majorana modes will require sophisticated spectroscopy and transport experiments, many of which are still under development.

If future work succeeds in stabilizing this exotic superconducting state at more accessible temperatures, the impact could be transformative. It would not only validate decades of theoretical work on unconventional superconductivity but also open a new frontier for devices that exploit the directional flow of quantum information. As the scientific community digests this unprecedented observation, the quest to control and harness broken time‑symmetry in superconductors is poised to become a central theme in condensed‑matter physics for years to come.
